
'''Kawachi no Ōkimi''' (河内王), also referred to as '''Kawachi-Ō''' (川内王), was a title borne by multiple {{ill|Imperial family|ja|皇族|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Imperial family|1=Imperial Family of Japan|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11581068}} members in ancient Japan. The name appears across different periods, from the {{ill|Asuka period|en|Asuka period|qid=Q210688|lt=Asuka period|1=Asuka period}} to the {{ill|Heian period|en|Heian period|qid=Q193292|lt=Heian period|1=Heian period}}, and refers to various individuals:

* An imperial prince of the {{ill|Asuka period|en|Asuka period|qid=Q210688|lt=Asuka period|1=Asuka period}}, serving as the {{ill|Dazai no Sochi|ja|筑紫大宰帥|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Governor-General of Tsukushi|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 大宰帥}} under {{ill|Empress Jitō|en|Empress Jitō|qid=Q232026|lt=Empress Jitō|1=Empress Jitō}}. See '''[[#Kawachi no Ōkimi (Asuka period)]]'''.
* An imperial prince of the early {{ill|Nara period|en|Nara period|qid=Q189178|lt=Nara period|1=Nara period}}, presumed to be the eldest son of {{ill|Prince Naga|en|Prince Naga|qid=Q3403340|lt=Prince Nagaya|1=Prince Naga}}. See '''[[#Kawachi no Ōkimi (Nara period)]]'''.
* An imperial prince of the late {{ill|Nara period|en|Nara period|qid=Q189178|lt=Nara period|1=Nara period}}, whose lineage is unclear. See '''{{ill|Kawachi no Ōkimi (Late Nara period)|ja|%E6%B2%B3%E5%86%85%E7%8E%8B_(%E5%A5%88%E8%89%AF%E6%99%82%E4%BB%A3%E5%BE%8C%E6%9C%9F)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kawachi no Ōkimi (Late Nara period)|qq=}}'''.
* A princess of the {{ill|Nara period|en|Nara period|qid=Q189178|lt=Nara period|1=Nara period}}, the daughter of {{ill|Prince Takechi|en|Prince Takechi|qid=Q837590|lt=Prince Takeda|1=Prince Takechi}} and a {{ill|Man'yōshū|en|Man'yōshū|qid=Q834321|lt=Man'yōshū|1=Man'yōshū}} poet. See '''{{ill|Kawachi no Joō|ja|%E6%B2%B3%E5%86%85%E5%A5%B3%E7%8E%8B|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kawachi no Joō|qq=}}'''.
* Other individuals bearing the title '''Kawachi no Ōkimi''' are known, but none are particularly notable.

== Kawachi no Ōkimi (Asuka period) ==
'''Kawachi no Ōkimi''' (birthdate unknown – April {{ill|694|en|694|qid=Q23483|lt=694|1=694}}) was an imperial prince of the {{ill|Asuka period|en|Asuka period|qid=Q210688|lt=Asuka period|1=Asuka period}}. Although his exact genealogy is not documented in reliable historical sources, analysis of texts like the {{ill|Shinsen Shōjiroku|en|Shinsen Shōjiroku|qid=Q1045362|lt=Shinsen Shōjiroku|1=Shinsen Shōjiroku}} suggests he was part of the lineage of {{ill|Prince Oshisaka Hikohito no Ōe|lt=Prince Oshisaka Hikohito no Ōe|lt=Prince Oshisaka no Hikohito no Oe|ja|押坂彦人大兄皇子|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Oshisaka no Hikohito no Oe|qq=}}, a descendant of {{ill|Emperor Bidatsu|en|Emperor Bidatsu|qid=Q316637|lt=Emperor Bidatsu|1=Emperor Bidatsu}}. Some interpretations suggest he was the son or grandson of {{ill|Prince Kudara|ja|百済王|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Kudara|1=Prince of Baekje|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11580788}}, who, despite his name, was not connected to the Korean kingdom of Baekje<ref>{{Cite news|author=|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141022115646/http://www.geocities.jp/namu_mauru/daiou6.htm|title=Ancient Japan and Korea|newspaper=|publisher=}}</ref>.

[[File:Tomb of Prince Kawachi.jpg|thumb|200px|Kawachi no Ōkimi's tomb site (Fukuoka Prefecture)<br>Includes the epitaph of Te-mochi Joō]]
In 686, he was dispatched to Tsukushi with {{ill|Otomo no Otomaro|ja|大伴安麻呂|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōtomo no Yasumaro|qq=}} and {{ill|Fujiwara no Ōshima|ja|中臣大嶋|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Fujiwara no Ōshima|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 中臣大島}} to receive {{ill|Silla envoy|lt=Silla envoy|lt=Envoys from Silla|ja|新羅使|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/envoys from Silla|qq=}}. In this capacity, he served as an intermediary for Emperor Tenmu. In 689, he was appointed {{ill|Dazai no Sochi|ja|筑紫大宰帥|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Governor-General of Tsukushi|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 大宰帥}} under {{ill|Empress Jitō|en|Empress Jitō|qid=Q232026|lt=Empress Jitō|1=Empress Jitō}}. In 690, he oversaw the hosting of Silla envoys. In 692, he dispatched Buddhist monks to spread Buddhism to Ōsumi Province and Ata Province, as well as ordered the presentation of an Amitābha statue.

In 694, he passed away in Tsukushi and was posthumously promoted to the Rank of {{ill|Senior Fourth Rank|ja|浄大肆|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Senior Fourth Rank|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}. His funeral rites were held at Mount Kagami in Bungo Province, as documented in three elegiac poems by his wife, {{ill|Te-mochi Joō|ja|手持女王|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Te-mochi Joō|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, found in the {{ill|Man'yōshū|en|Man'yōshū|qid=Q834321|lt=Man'yōshū|1=Man'yōshū}}, Volume 3 (poems 417–419). His supposed tomb, the Kogane Kofun in Kawaran-machi, Fukuoka Prefecture, was designated as his burial site by the {{ill|Ministry of the Imperial Household|en|Ministry of the Imperial Household|qid=Q8193428|lt=Ministry of the Imperial Household|1=Ministry of the Imperial Household}} in 1894.

== Kawachi no Ōkimi (Nara period) ==
'''Kawachi no Ōkimi''' (birthdate unknown – July {{ill|728|en|728|qid=Q23560|lt=728|1=728}}), active during the {{ill|Nara period|en|Nara period|qid=Q189178|lt=Nara period|1=Nara period}}, was the eldest son of {{ill|Prince Naga|en|Prince Naga|qid=Q3403340|lt=Prince Nagaya|1=Prince Naga}}. In {{ill|714|en|714|qid=Q23525|lt=714|1=714}}, he was promoted from {{ill|Unranked|ja|无位|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Unranked|qq=}} to {{ill|Junior Fourth Rank|lt=Junior Fourth Rank, Lower Grade|ja|従四位下|lt=Junior Fourth Rank, Lower Grade|1=Junior Fourth Rank|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Junior Fourth Rank|13=User:Immanuelle/Junior Fourth Rank|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 従四位}} as a grandson of Emperor Tenmu. He passed away in 728 without leaving significant achievements.

While the ''Kōin Shōunroku'' lists him as the father of Prince Takayasu and his brothers, these claims conflict with primary sources.<ref>Sawada Hiroshi, "Genealogy of Tenmu's Imperial Relatives" (''Kokushi Gaku'', No. 142, 1990)</ref>

The genealogical relationship between the two individuals known as Kawachi no Ōkimi has historically been confused, with figures such as {{ill|Prince Takechi|en|Prince Takechi|qid=Q837590|lt=Prince Takeda|1=Prince Takechi}} and his descendants inaccurately merged into their lineage.

== Genealogical Confusion ==
Genealogical confusion arose from sources such as the {{ill|Honchō Kōin Shōunroku|ja|本朝皇胤紹運録|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Honchō Kōin Shōunroku|qq=}}, which merged the two individuals into a single lineage. The record erroneously placed {{ill|Prince Takeda's descendants|ja|Emperor Tenmu|1=Emperor Tenmu|2=ja|3=天武天皇|1=Emperor Tenmu|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Takeda's descendants|13=User:Immanuelle/Emperor Tenmu|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q335181}} into the lineage of Kawachi no Ōkimi of the {{ill|Asuka period|en|Asuka period|qid=Q210688|lt=Asuka period|1=Asuka period}}, including figures like {{ill|Prince Takeda|ja|大原高安|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Takeda|1=Takayasu Ohara|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q17989661}}, {{ill|Prince Sakurai|ja|桜井王|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Sakurai|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 大原桜井}}, and {{ill|Prince Kadobe|ja|門部王|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Kadobe|1=Prince Kadobe|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q27501187}}.

Modern scholars, including Tanaka Taku, have reconstructed the genealogies to distinguish between the two individuals, separating the lines into those descended from {{ill|Emperor Bidatsu|en|Emperor Bidatsu|qid=Q316637|lt=Emperor Bidatsu|1=Emperor Bidatsu}} and those descended from {{ill|Emperor Tenmu|1=Emperor Tenmu|2=ja|3=天武天皇|ja|Emperor Tenmu|1=Emperor Tenmu|2=ja|3=天武天皇|1=Emperor Tenmu|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Emperor Tenmu|13=User:Immanuelle/Emperor Tenmu|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q335181}}<ref>Tanaka Taku, "On the Debate Concerning Prince Kibi," *Collected Works of Tanaka Taku,* Vol. 5, Kokusho Kankōkai, 1985.</ref>.
